title: Against Celsus, Book IV
blurb: Origen answers Celsus’s scorn for the belief that God or his Son comes down to the world, showing that the Word comes down without change and that God’s threats and punishments are a cure, not a fit of temper. He then defends the stories of Genesis and the patriarchs, read in their deeper sense, against the charge that they are silly tales, and rejects Celsus’s claim that the world was made no more for man than for the animals, which Celsus thought nearer to God than men.
first_english_note: Earlier English: Frederick Crombie (Ante-Nicene Fathers, 1872) and Henry Chadwick (1953). This is a fresh English translation from Koetschau's Greek; neither was used as wording.

text_history.method: Translated from the Greek of Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI, which serves as the copy-text. Each chapter was translated from the Greek and then checked clause by clause against it in a separate review. No earlier English translation was consulted.
